title: What is a String in Java — a sequence of characters, immutable (cannot be changed after creation).
shortTitle: What is a String in Java

s1_definition.profdef: A `String` in Java is an object that represents a sequence of characters. Its defining property is immutability: once a String object is created, its contents can never change. Every operation that appears to modify a String, such as `concat` or `toUpperCase`, actually returns a brand new String and leaves the original untouched. String literals are interned in the String pool so identical literals share one object.
s1_definition.analogy: A String is like a printed cheque at National Bank of India. Once the cheque is printed with "Rajesh Kumar" and an amount, you cannot erase and rewrite it. If you need a different amount, you print a new cheque. The old cheque still exists exactly as printed. That is why a String never changes — any "change" produces a new String, like printing a fresh cheque.
s1_definition.oneliner: A String is an immutable sequence of characters — you never change it, you only create a new one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A `String` in Java is an object that represents a sequence of characters. Its defining property is immutability: once a String object is created, its contents can never change. Every operation that appears to modify a String, such as `concat` or `toUpperCase`, actually returns a brand new String and leaves the original untouched. String literals are interned in the String pool so identical literals share one object.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A String is like a printed cheque at National Bank of India. Once the cheque is printed with "Rajesh Kumar" and an amount, you cannot erase and rewrite it. If you need a different amount, you print a new cheque. The old cheque still exists exactly as printed. That is why a String never changes — any "change" produces a new String, like printing a fresh cheque.

**One line to remember:** A String is an immutable sequence of characters — you never change it, you only create a new one.

sections.s2_technical:
Internally a modern Java String wraps a byte array holding the characters plus an encoding flag, and it is declared `final` so the class cannot be subclassed and the backing data cannot be reassigned. Because the contents never change, Strings are safe to share freely across threads without any synchronisation, and they are safe to use as keys in a HashMap because their hash code never changes after creation.

Immutability is why String operations return new objects. For example `String masked = accountId.substring(0, 2) + "XXXX";` builds a new String; `accountId` itself is unchanged. Similarly `name.toUpperCase()` returns a new uppercase String and leaves `name` alone. If you ignore the returned value, nothing appears to happen, which is the classic beginner bug: writing `name.trim();` on its own line does nothing useful because you discarded the new String.

Java maintains a String pool. String literals like `"SAV2001"` written in code are interned, so two identical literals refer to the same object, and `==` between them is true. But Strings created with `new String("SAV2001")` are distinct objects, so you must always compare String contents with `.equals()`, never with `==`. When you build a String in a loop, repeated concatenation creates many throwaway objects, so you use a mutable `StringBuilder` instead for efficiency, then call `toString()` once at the end.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India must mask Rajesh's account id on screen, showing only the first two characters and hiding the rest, like "SAXXXX". The system takes the original id and produces a masked version. This is exactly how String immutability works — masking does not change the stored id, it produces a new masked String, so the real id in memory stays intact for audit.

Problem 2 — When the system reads an account id from a web form and compares it with the stored id, using the wrong comparison would silently fail. This is exactly why we compare Strings with equals, not with double-equals, because two Strings with the same characters can be different objects in memory.

The code has an `AccountMasker` class with a `mask` method that returns a new masked String, and a `matches` method that compares using equals. The demo masks Rajesh's id and shows the original is unchanged.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: `accountId = "SAV2001"`.

Step 1 — `mask` validates the id is long enough. It is.

Step 2 — `substring(0, 2)` produces a new String `"SA"`. The original `"SAV2001"` is untouched.

Step 3 — Concatenating `"SA" + "XXXX"` produces another new String `"SAXXXX"`, which is returned.

Step 4 — We log the original and see it still reads `"SAV2001"`, proving immutability.

Step 5 — We create `fromForm` with `new String("SAV2001")`, a different object with the same characters. `matches` uses `equals` and returns true, while `==` returns false because they are different objects.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A String in Java is an object representing a sequence of characters, and its single most important property is immutability. Once a String is created, its contents can never change. Every method that looks like it modifies a String, such as substring, concat, or toUpperCase, actually returns a brand new String and leaves the original completely untouched. The String class is declared final, so it cannot be subclassed, and its backing data cannot be reassigned.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, this property is what makes PII masking safe. When I mask Rajesh's account id to show only the first two characters, the masking produces a new String, and the real account id stored in memory and the database is never altered, which is important for auditing. I rely on the same property to share Strings freely across threads without synchronisation, and to use Strings as HashMap keys, because an immutable object has a hash code that never changes after creation.

The practical consequence I always highlight is comparison. Because a String literal written in code is interned in the String pool while a String created with the new keyword is a separate object, two Strings can hold the same characters but be different objects in memory. So I always compare String contents with the equals method, never with the double-equals operator, because double-equals compares object identity and would silently fail when a value read from a web form does not happen to be the same pooled object as the stored value. I also use a StringBuilder when I build a String in a loop, because repeated concatenation of immutable Strings creates many throwaway objects.
